excerpt: Lost wages and lost earning capacity are different claims. How to prove each after an injury in Georgia or South Carolina, and what documentation you need.
keyTakeaways: Lost wages and lost earning capacity are two distinct categories of economic damages recoverable in Georgia and South Carolina personal injury cases. Lost wages cover income already missed during recovery, while lost earning capacity addresses permanent reductions in future income. Georgia's 2-year statute of limitations (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33) and modified comparative fault rule (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33) allow recovery if less than 50% at fault. South Carolina gives 3 years (S.C. Code § 15-3-530) with a 51% fault threshold. Self-employed and gig workers can recover using tax returns, contracts, and financial records.

faqs.question: What is the difference between lost wages and lost earning capacity?
faqs.answer: Lost wages are income you already missed while recovering from your injuries. Lost earning capacity is a forward-looking claim for future income you will never earn because your injuries permanently reduced your ability to work. Both are recoverable in Georgia and South Carolina personal injury cases, but they require different types of proof and expert analysis.

faqs.question: How do I prove lost wages in a personal injury claim?
faqs.answer: You will need documentation from your employer confirming your pay rate, hours missed, and reason for absence. Key evidence includes pay stubs, W-2s, tax returns, a verification letter from your employer, and a doctor's note connecting your absence to accident injuries. Self-employed workers can use tax returns, profit-and-loss statements, contracts, and client communications.

faqs.question: Can I recover lost wages if I used sick days or vacation time?
faqs.answer: Yes. In both Georgia and South Carolina, you can recover compensation for paid time off you were forced to use because of your accident injuries. Those sick days and vacation days have monetary value, and you should not have to deplete your benefits because of someone else's negligence.

faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a lost wage claim in Georgia?
faqs.answer: Georgia's statute of limitations for personal injury claims, including lost wages, is 2 years from the date of injury under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. If you miss this deadline, you lose the right to recover any compensation. Lost earning capacity claims follow the same 2-year deadline.

faqs.question: What is the statute of limitations for a lost wage claim in South Carolina?
faqs.answer: South Carolina gives you 3 years from the date of injury to file a personal injury claim under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. This applies to all damages including lost wages and lost earning capacity. Filing promptly is still advisable because evidence fades and witnesses become harder to locate over time.

faqs.question: How does comparative fault affect my lost wage recovery?
faqs.answer: In Georgia, your lost wage award is reduced by your percentage of fault, and you recover nothing if you are 50% or more at fault (O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33). In South Carolina, the threshold is 51% — you can recover as long as your fault does not equal or exceed 51%. Both states reduce your total award proportionally to your share of blame.
